0.msg: What age do required withdrawals from my retirement accounts start?
0.text: Required withdrawals from retirement accounts start at age 73 under the current IRS rule. If you reach age 72 after December 31, 2022, your first withdrawal is due by April 1 of the year after you reach 73, and later withdrawals are due by December 31 each year. If a required withdrawal is too small, the IRS may charge a 25% excise tax on the amount missed (IRS Publication 590-B).

4.msg: When can I sign up for Medicare?
4.text: You can sign up for Medicare generally when you turn 65. Your Initial Enrollment Period lasts 7 months, starting 3 months before the month you turn 65 and ending 3 months after that month. The plan uses age 65 as the Medicare age, so you would be about 31 years away from it, since you are 34 now. If you miss this window, you may have to wait and pay a monthly late penalty for as long as you have Part B.

6.msg: How much can I put in an IRA each year?
6.text: The IRA limit is $7,500 a year. If you are 50 or older, you can add a catch-up of $1,100, for $8,600 a year in total. These limits apply to IRAs in general, so they are the same for 2027 as the IRS listed them. Your plan is based on $14,000 a year going into your 401(k), so your IRA room is separate from that.

8.msg: What happens to my plan if inflation runs high?
8.text: You can count on $111,300 a year: $48,600 for basics and $62,700 for the rest. First step: Keep about 49% of savings in stocks now. We tried 5 plans of households like yours and several simple plans on your numbers. The plan of a couple aged 71 and 68, retired, with about $1,000,000 saved kept your basics safest and left the most to spend.

9.msg: Will Medicare pay for a nursing home?
9.text: The passages I found do not say that Medicare pays for a nursing home stay in general. They only cover when Medicare coverage starts and how late sign-up penalties work, so I cannot confirm what Medicare pays for nursing home care. Your plan does not show Medicare paying for this care either. It plans for long-term care at about $129575 per year for 3 years, so you should plan for that cost from your own savings and other sources.

11.msg: What does 'covered in 90 of 100 futures' mean?
11.text: "N of 100" means this: we ran your plan through 100 different paths that markets might take, and in N of them the money lasted. Markets are uncertain, so these are chances, not promises. A higher number is safer.

12.msg: Why is the amount I can count on lower than what I want to spend?

16.msg: What is the biggest risk to my plan?
16.text: The plan's biggest risk is that it falls short of your goal. It shows your savings run out at age 76 if you spend $85,000 a year, which is about $17,300 a year more than your safe spending of about $67,700. Your basic costs are covered in full, so the gap is in the extra spending you want. You can close it by saving more, retiring later, or lowering the spending goal. The plan also shows you have no life insurance cover, with a gap of $1,100,000, so your family would have no income if something happened to you.
